plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks two panels, labeled (a) and (b), each plotting projectile trajectories that leave and return to the same level ground line. In panel (a) three parabolic arcs share one launch point and an angle marked 45 degrees, distinguished by velocity arrows at the origin labeled 30 m/s in orange, 40 m/s in purple, and 50 m/s in teal; a key at the upper right shows y up and x right. Dashed verticals drop from each apex, and three dimension bars beneath the ground line read R = 91.8 m, R = 163 m, and R = 255 m in that same order. Panel (b) instead fixes the speed, labeled v0 = 50 m/s, and varies the angle, with nested arcs at the origin marking 15, 45, and 75 degrees; only two dimension bars appear, R = 128 m ending at a dashed vertical where both the 15-degree and 75-degree curves land, and R = 255 m spanning the 45-degree curve. Matching each color-coded launch arrow to its own range bar isolates one launch parameter at a time. The layout supports the range relationship, in which range grows with the square of initial speed, peaks at 45 degrees, and repeats for complementary angles whose apex heights differ.

demo_steps.title: One launch, one parabola
demo_steps.narration: A projectile leaves the origin at 30 m/s and 45° and returns to the same ground line 91.8 m away. The dashed line marks its apex; the bar below measures its range.

demo_steps.title: More speed, much more range
demo_steps.narration: Raise v₀ to 40 m/s: the angle is unchanged, but the range jumps to 163 m — far more than the 33% speed increase would suggest.

demo_steps.title: Range scales as v₀²
demo_steps.narration: At 50 m/s the projectile reaches 255 m. Comparing 30, 40 and 50 m/s shows the ranges scale like 9 : 16 : 25 — exactly the squares of the speeds.

demo_steps.title: Now hold speed, sweep the angle
demo_steps.narration: Switch to panel (b): v₀ is locked at 50 m/s. A shallow 15° launch gives a flat arc that lands at 128 m.

demo_steps.title: 45° maximizes the range
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ upward: the range grows to a maximum of 255 m at 45°, then falls again as the arc becomes steep and tall.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share a landing point
demo_steps.narration: At 75° the projectile climbs much higher and hangs much longer, yet it lands at the very same 128 m as the 15° shot — complementary angles give equal range.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Range obeys R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g: speed enters squared (so it dominates), while the angle enters only through sin(2θ), which peaks at 45° and takes the same value for θ and 90° − θ.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing a visual language, each with a single horizontal ground line and a common launch point at the far left. Curves are smooth parabolas that start and end on the ground line, drawn in the textbook's three colors: orange (slowest / shallowest), purple (middle), teal (fastest / steepest). Short color-matched velocity arrows fan out from the origin with text labels ('30 m/s', '40 m/s', '50 m/s' in panel a; 'v₀ = 50 m/s' with nested arcs '15°', '45°', '75°' in panel b); panel (a) has a single arc labeled '45°' since all three share the angle. Thin gray dashed verticals drop from each apex (panel a) and from the shared 15°/75° landing point and the tall 75° apex (panel b). Below the ground line, stacked horizontal dimension bars with arrowheads and end ticks carry centered labels 'R = 91.8 m', 'R = 163 m', 'R = 255 m' in panel (a) and 'R = 128 m', 'R = 255 m' in panel (b); bar lengths must match the landing x-positions of their curves. A small y-up / x-right axis key sits at the upper right of panel (a); italic '(a)' and '(b)' captions sit centered beneath each panel. In the interactive version the textbook curves remain as faint reference ghosts while the learner-controlled trajectory is drawn bold with a filled landing dot, a live apex dashed line, and its own dimension bar that stretches in real time; a compact readout shows v₀, θ, R, max height and flight time. Both panels use the same horizontal scale so a 255 m range is visually identical across panels.

authoredContext:
Note particularly that the equation is valid only for launch and impact on a horizontal surface. We see the range is directly proportional to the square of the initial speed v0 and sin2θ0, and it is inversely proportional to the acceleration of gravity. Thus, on the Moon, the range would be six times greater than on Earth for the same initial velocity. Furthermore, we see from the factor sin2θ0 that the range is maximum at 45°. These results are shown in the figure. In (a) we see that the greater the initial velocity, the greater the range. In (b), we see that the range is maximum at 45°. This is true only for conditions neglecting air resistance. If air resistance is considered, the maximum angle is somewhat smaller. It is interesting that the same range is found for two initial launch angles that sum to 90°. The projectile launched with the smaller angle has a lower apex than the higher angle, but they both have the same range.

Trajectories of projectiles on level ground. (a) The greater the initial speed v0, the greater the range for a given initial angle. (b) The effect of initial angle θ0 on the range of a projectile with a given initial speed. Note that the range is the same for initial angles of 15° and 75°, although the maximum heights of those paths are different.

Figure a shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial 45 degree angle above the horizontal and different initial velocities. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for 30 meters per second, giving a range R (distance from launch to landing) of 91.8 m. In purple is the trajectory for 40 meters per second, giving a range R of 163 m. In blue is the trajectory for 50 meters per second, giving a range R of 255 m. The maximum height of the projectile increases with initial speed. Figure b shows the trajectories of projectiles launched at the same initial speed of 50 meters per second and different launch angles. The trajectories are shown from launch to landing back at the initial elevation. In orange is the trajectory for an angle of 15 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m. In purple is the trajectory for an angle of 45 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 255 m. In blue is the trajectory for an angle of 75 degrees above the horizontal, giving a range R of 128 m, the same as for the 15 degree trajectory. The maximum height increases with launch angle.

When we speak of the range of a projectile on level ground, we assume R is very small compared with the circumference of Earth. If, however, the range is large, Earth curves away below the projectile and the acceleration resulting from gravity changes direction along the path. The range is larger than predicted by the range equation given earlier because the projectile has farther to fall than it would on level ground, as shown in the figure, which is based on a drawing in Newton’s Principia. If the initial speed is great enough, the projectile goes into orbit. Earth’s surface drops 5 m every 8000 m. In 1 s an object falls 5 m without air resistance. Thus, if an object is given a horizontal velocity of 8000 m/s (or 18,000 mi/hr) near Earth’s surface, it will go into orbit around the planet because the surface continuously falls away from the object. This is roughly the speed of the Space Shuttle in a low Earth orbit when it was operational, or any satellite in a low Earth orbit. These and other aspects of orbital motion, such as Earth’s rotation, are covered in greater depth in Gravitation.

plan.concept: For a projectile launched and landing at the same height, horizontal range depends on launch speed squared and on sin(2θ) — so range grows quadratically with v₀ at fixed angle, peaks at 45°, and is identical for complementary angles that reach very different heights.

demo_steps.title: One launch, one parabola
demo_steps.narration: A projectile leaves the origin at 30 m/s and 45° and returns to the same ground line 91.8 m away. The dashed line marks its apex; the bar below measures its range.

demo_steps.title: More speed, much more range
demo_steps.narration: Raise v₀ to 40 m/s: the angle is unchanged, but the range jumps to 163 m — far more than the 33% speed increase would suggest.

demo_steps.title: Range scales as v₀²
demo_steps.narration: At 50 m/s the projectile reaches 255 m. Comparing 30, 40 and 50 m/s shows the ranges scale like 9 : 16 : 25 — exactly the squares of the speeds.

demo_steps.title: Now hold speed, sweep the angle
demo_steps.narration: Switch to panel (b): v₀ is locked at 50 m/s. A shallow 15° launch gives a flat arc that lands at 128 m.

demo_steps.title: 45° maximizes the range
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ upward: the range grows to a maximum of 255 m at 45°, then falls again as the arc becomes steep and tall.

demo_steps.title: Complementary angles share a landing point
demo_steps.narration: At 75° the projectile climbs much higher and hangs much longer, yet it lands at the very same 128 m as the 15° shot — complementary angles give equal range.

plan.keyInsight: Range obeys R = v₀²sin(2θ)/g: speed enters squared (so it dominates), while the angle enters only through sin(2θ), which peaks at 45° and takes the same value for θ and 90° − θ.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing a visual language, each with a single horizontal ground line and a common launch point at the far left. Curves are smooth parabolas that start and end on the ground line, drawn in the textbook's three colors: orange (slowest / shallowest), purple (middle), teal (fastest / steepest). Short color-matched velocity arrows fan out from the origin with text labels ('30 m/s', '40 m/s', '50 m/s' in panel a; 'v₀ = 50 m/s' with nested arcs '15°', '45°', '75°' in panel b); panel (a) has a single arc labeled '45°' since all three share the angle. Thin gray dashed verticals drop from each apex (panel a) and from the shared 15°/75° landing point and the tall 75° apex (panel b). Below the ground line, stacked horizontal dimension bars with arrowheads and end ticks carry centered labels 'R = 91.8 m', 'R = 163 m', 'R = 255 m' in panel (a) and 'R = 128 m', 'R = 255 m' in panel (b); bar lengths must match the landing x-positions of their curves. A small y-up / x-right axis key sits at the upper right of panel (a); italic '(a)' and '(b)' captions sit centered beneath each panel. In the interactive version the textbook curves remain as faint reference ghosts while the learner-controlled trajectory is drawn bold with a filled landing dot, a live apex dashed line, and its own dimension bar that stretches in real time; a compact readout shows v₀, θ, R, max height and flight time. Both panels use the same horizontal scale so a 255 m range is visually identical across panels.
